exercise-library: Tap Chest, Back, Shoulders, Arms, Legs and glutes, Core, Cardio or Stretching, or leave it on All to scroll through every group on one page.
Filter by equipment (none, dumbbell, barbell, machine or cable) and by level, or search for an exercise or a muscle such as squat or biceps.

fitnessExerciseLibrary.title: Exercise Library
fitnessExerciseLibrary.subtitle: Browse gym and home exercises by body area, with moving pictures and step-by-step instructions. Filter by equipment and level. Free, no sign-up.
faq: Where do the pictures and instructions come from?

They come from the free-exercise-db project, an open dataset released into the public domain. Each exercise has a photo of the start position and a photo of the end position. This page fades between the two so the movement is easy to follow. We chose about 140 common exercises from the larger dataset.
Is this medical advice? Are these exercises right for me?

No. This is general information and not medical advice. If you are injured, pregnant, recovering from surgery, have a heart, joint or blood-pressure condition, or have not exercised for a long time, talk to a doctor or a qualified trainer before you start. Begin with a light weight, keep good form and stop if you feel sharp pain, dizziness or chest discomfort.
How many sets and reps should I do?

It depends on your goal and level. Many beginners start with two or three sets of eight to twelve repetitions, using a weight that makes the last few repetitions hard while keeping good form. Lower repetitions with heavier weights build strength, and higher repetitions with lighter weights build muscular endurance. A trainer can set numbers for your body and goals.
How often should I train each muscle?

A common guideline is to train each major muscle group about two times a week and to leave a day or two of rest before working the same muscles hard again. Spread your sessions across the week, for example upper body, lower body and core on different days, or a full body session on alternate days.
Can I use this at home without a gym?

Yes. Set the equipment filter to No equipment for bodyweight exercises such as push-ups, squats, lunges, planks and bridges, or to Dumbbell if you own a pair. The Stretching group needs no equipment either.
What is the difference between the Cardio and the strength groups?

Cardio exercises keep your heart rate raised for a longer time, for example cycling, rowing, jogging, skipping or jumping moves. Strength exercises work muscles against resistance, in short sets with rests in between. A balanced week usually includes both, plus stretching.
Is my information uploaded or stored?
No. Searching and filtering happen in your browser and nothing you type is sent to {{siteName}}. The page still loads the exercise pictures, advertising and other resources from the network.

sections.heading: What the library covers
paragraphs: The library lists about 140 common exercises in eight groups: chest, back, shoulders, arms, legs and glutes, core, cardio and stretching. For every exercise you see the muscles it mainly works, the muscles that help, the equipment it needs, a level from beginner to advanced and numbered steps.

Each picture shows two positions and fades between them in a loop, so you can see the start, the movement and the finish without playing a video. If your device is set to reduce motion, the pictures stay still and show the start position.

sections.heading: Putting a balanced session together
paragraphs: A simple full body session picks one exercise from each of a few areas: a press for the chest or shoulders, a pull for the back, a squat or lunge for the legs, and one core exercise. Pairing pushing and pulling movements keeps the shoulders balanced, and finishing with core work and a short stretch rounds off the session.
If you train at home, filter by No equipment first and add a pair of dumbbells later. If you use a gym, machines and cables are a gentle way to learn a movement before you move to free weights.

sections.heading: Warming up and cooling down
paragraphs: Spend five to ten minutes before lifting on easy cardio such as cycling or brisk walking, and on a few mobility moves from the Stretching group, such as arm circles and hip circles. After training, slower stretches for the muscles you used help you wind down.
Stretching does not replace rest. Sleep, enough food and a day or two between hard sessions for the same muscles matter as much as the exercises themselves.

sections.heading: Staying safe
paragraphs: Good form matters more than heavy weight. Learn each movement with a light weight or none at all, control the weight on the way down, and breathe steadily instead of holding your breath. Ask a trainer to check your form on the big lifts such as squats and deadlifts.

Stop and rest if you feel sharp pain, dizziness or chest discomfort, and speak to a doctor about it. The photos and steps come from an open dataset, so they are a starting point and not a replacement for personal coaching.
